newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk MPs say coalition reluctant in scandal probe.
newsitem.headline: Turk MPs say coalition reluctant in scandal probe.

text.p: Turkish opposition MPs said in a report presented on Wednesday that the Islamist-led coalition only reluctantly pursued a parliamentary inquiry into links between top officials and right-wing gangsters.

"As time passed it was seen that the government did not support the will towards setting up the commission in order to inquire and investigate the events," said the report by two Motherland Party (ANAP) deputies who took part in the inquiry.
"(They supported it because) of the inability to stop the public's unavoidable, considerable outrage about the events."
The ANAP deputies previously withdrew their support for the official inquiry report and presented their own investigation to the deputy speaker of parliament on Wednesday.

The official report accused two Turkish government MPs of deep involvement in the security scandal, which was sparked after a senior policeman, a fugitive gangster and a former beauty queen died in the same car in a traffic accident last November. Guns and silencers were found in the wreckage.

Deputies Mehmet Agar and Sedat Bucak, from the right-wing True Path Party (DYP), face charges over the scandal. Bucak heads a Kurdish anti-rebel militia and was a passenger in the car. The two men, who deny any wrongdoing, face more than five years in jail for forming a criminal gang and sheltering Abdullah Catli, the gangster who died in the crash.
A court's bid to lift the MPs' parliamentary immunity has been delayed for more than two months by the office of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, Islamist Welfare Party (RP) leader.
The ANAP deputies' report criticised the inquiry for backing down from questioning deputy prime minister and DYP leader, Tansu Ciller, and her businessman husband over the scandal.

"Pressure was brought to bear on the RP members who cast a conscience vote on calling the Cillers," the report said. It said the four-month investigation had unearthed contradictions in officials' statements which required further investigation.
Last November's crash and its aftermath revealed an intricate web of drug smuggling, arms trafficking and illegal killings, according to the RP deputy who headed the inquiry.

The probe said in the final report that right-wing militants contracted by Turkey after a 1980 coup to carry out political dirty work at home and abroad used official protection to smuggle drugs, murder business opponents and launder money.
The official inquiry's report is due to be heard in parliament but MPs do not have to act on any of its findings.

The report said organised crime spread through southeast Turkey in the 1990s under the cover of the fight against the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party. Many pro-government Kurdish village guards are involved in common crime, it said.
